title: "Setup"
subtitle: "Day 0 — the evening of 6 August 2026. About an hour, and it is the difference between day 1 being a study day and day 1 being an afternoon of dependency errors."
---

Nothing here is hard. It is here so that no day in the next year begins with an install.

## The environment

You already have `uv` from the LLM bootcamp. A separate environment, because the two courses pin
different things and you do not want a PyTorch upgrade to break a backtest in March.

```bash
uv venv ~/.venvs/quant --python 3.12
source ~/.venvs/quant/bin/activate
```

Then the core stack. This is the whole list for weeks 1 through 20; the derivatives and C++ tooling
arrives when you need it, in phase 8 and phase 10.

```bash
uv pip install --python ~/.venvs/quant/bin/python \
  numpy pandas polars pyarrow duckdb scipy statsmodels scikit-learn \
  matplotlib seaborn jupyterlab \
  arch linearmodels cvxpy \
  yfinance pandas-datareader requests \
  pytest ruff
```

What each of those is for, so that none of it is cargo cult:

| Package | Why it is in the list |
|:--|:--|
| `duckdb` + `pyarrow` | Your data store. SQL directly over Parquet files, no server. It doubles as the place you learn SQL properly in week 45. |
| `polars` | For anything large or repeated. Keep pandas too — most quant code you will ever read is pandas. |
| `statsmodels` | Time series, state space and the Kalman filter. `statsmodels.tsa` and `statsmodels.statespace` are weeks 10–14. |
| `arch` | Kevin Sheppard's package. GARCH, unit-root tests, the bootstrap, and the Reality Check / SPA tests you need in week 8. |
| `linearmodels` | Also Sheppard's. Panel models, IV/2SLS and Fama-MacBeth regressions. The IV code will look familiar. |
| `cvxpy` | Convex optimization. Phase 4 writes portfolio constraints by hand rather than calling a black box. |
| `yfinance` | Free daily bars, good enough to learn on. It is unofficial and personal-use only — week 3 covers what it gets wrong and what replaces it. |

## Accounts

Five minutes each, and every one is free. Do these tonight because two of them take a day to approve.

- **[Alpaca](https://alpaca.markets/)** — free paper trading and a market-data API. This is the broker
  the running strategy eventually trades against. Sign up now; the account is used from week 3 and
  seriously from week 47.
- **[Nasdaq Data Link](https://data.nasdaq.com/)** — free API key, used for some of the reference datasets.
- **[Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/)** — several past competitions (Optiver realized volatility, Jane
  Street market prediction) released real data that phases 6 and 7 use as a proving ground.
- **[Numerai](https://numer.ai/)** — a free tournament on obfuscated financial data with real payouts.
  You will submit to it from phase 7, and it is the one public track record that quant employers
  actually recognise.
- **[Interactive Brokers](https://www.interactivebrokers.com/)** — optional and slower to open. Their
  paper account is the more realistic execution environment if you want it in phase 10.

You do not need a Bloomberg terminal, a paid data subscription, or a broker with real money in it. Not
this year.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Check whether UW-Madison licenses WRDS.** If it does, you get CRSP and Compustat — survivorship-free
US equity history with point-in-time fundamentals, which is the single largest data-quality upgrade
available to you and costs an institution tens of thousands of dollars a year. Ask the business school
library. Week 3 assumes free data and tells you what it is missing; if WRDS comes through, that week
gets much better.
:::

## Two repositories

Same split that worked for the LLM bootcamp: the plan is one repo, the work is another.

```
projects/
├── quant-365-day-bootcamp/    this site, and data/schedule.yml
└── quant-365-work/            your notebooks, code and reports  ← work here
```

Create the work repo now, private, and give it this shape:

```
quant-365-work/
├── env.sh                  activates ~/.venvs/quant and sets QUANT_DATA
├── data/                   gitignored — parquet, duckdb files, downloads
├── notebooks/              one per day, named by day number
├── qlib/                   the package you actually build: ingest, signals, backtest, exec
├── reports/                the twelve milestone documents
└── tests/
```

Name notebooks by day — `notebooks/day-047-sharpe-standard-error.ipynb` — because on day 203 a milestone
report needs a result from week 7 and you will not remember which week it was.

**Gitignore the data.** Commit the query, the date range, the universe definition and the seed. Never the
Parquet files. You already work this way with genotype data; the reasoning is identical and the file
sizes are smaller.

## What a year of data actually costs you in disk

Plan for this now so week 3 does not surprise you.

| What | Roughly |
|:--|:--|
| Daily bars, ~5,000 US equities and ETFs, 20 years | 2–4 GB as Parquet |
| Minute bars, ~500 names, 5 years | 40–80 GB |
| One month of full order book for one liquid crypto pair | 20–60 GB |
| Ken French factor returns, FRED series, everything in phase 2 | under 100 MB |

Phases 1 through 8 fit comfortably in the first row. Only phase 9 needs the third, and only for a few
symbols and a few days.

## Verify

If this prints a table of returns and a Sharpe ratio, you are ready for day 1.

```python
import duckdb, yfinance as yf, numpy as np

px = yf.download("SPY", start="2015-01-01", end="2025-01-01", auto_adjust=True)["Close"]
r = np.log(px / px.shift(1)).dropna()

print(f"{len(r)} daily observations, {r.index[0].date()} to {r.index[-1].date()}")
print(f"annualised mean  {r.mean() * 252:.3f}")
print(f"annualised vol   {r.std() * np.sqrt(252):.3f}")
print(f"Sharpe (rf = 0)  {r.mean() / r.std() * np.sqrt(252):.3f}")
print(duckdb.sql("select 42 as duckdb_works").fetchall())
```

Three things about that snippet are wrong or misleading, and you will be able to name all three by day
50. `auto_adjust=True` is doing something to the price history that week 3 makes you look at. The Sharpe
ratio has no standard error attached, which week 7 fixes. And `rf = 0` was defensible in 2021 and is not
now. Leave the code as it is; it is a marker.

## Where the year's reading comes from

Most of the resources are free — MIT OpenCourseWare, QuantEcon, Ken French's data library, arXiv, and
the free lecture notes from Oxford, Princeton and NYU. Some are not, and the paid ones are concentrated
in two places:

- **Phase 8 (derivatives)** leans on Shreve and on Hull. Free lecture notes cover most of it, and the
  day pages name them, but if you buy one book for this year, buy Shreve volume II.
- **Phase 11 (the interview)** leans on the Green Book and *Heard on the Street*. There is no free
  substitute of comparable quality, they are cheap, and you will use them for fifty drill sittings.

Everything else has a free path. Where a day depends on a paid book, it names a free alternative in the
same resource list.

## One honest warning before day 1

You are about to spend 365 hours on a field that is unusually good at producing convincing-looking
results that are not real. The single most valuable thing you bring is the instinct that a striking
result is probably a multiple-testing artifact until shown otherwise — you have that instinct because
genome-wide association studies had their own reckoning with it a decade before you arrived.

Keep it. Phases 2 and 5 exist to make it quantitative, and by phase 6 it will be the thing that
distinguishes your research from most of what gets published in this field.
